Telos is the general agent execution layer of the SSCCS stack. Actus plans
with the LLM; Telos converts plans into system effects. A command arrives,
a coordinate is resolved, a process or file or network effect happens, and
the result returns. The layer is general: it executes without binding to a
language or a domain.

Telos is a headless agent in the form of a single native binary of about
seventy megabytes. There is no interface to launch, no runtime to install,
and no daemon to supervise; the binary is the entire deployment unit. It
runs on any machine that can execute it, serves a project from its root,
and scales into a fleet of coordinated nodes.

The working thesis is that an agent does not need to traverse trees to act.
Work is addressed by coordinate and reached by teleport: no directory
descent, no sequential scans. The agent moves between work locations in
space, and the execution layer materializes that movement as concrete
system calls, tool invocations, and protocol traffic over files, processes,
and networks.

**tel: an agent per project, one command away.**

## Native Execution

Telos is a native binary. The agent core runs on OS threads with
ownership-checked parallelism, so CPU-bound work such as parsing, indexing,
and large-scale analysis uses every core it is given.

- Single binary, no dependencies: one file is the entire deployment unit,
  and the node runs wherever the file runs.
- Multithreaded by construction: the agent loop, language analysis, LSP
  traffic, and tool execution share a native thread pool instead of
  contending for one lock or one event loop.
- Ownership-checked parallelism: the compiler rules out the data races
  that interpreted runtimes discover only at runtime.
- Bounded resources: each node owns its memory space and thread pool, so
  resource use stays predictable under load.

## The Fleet

```{python}
    nexus -> node_b [label="strengthen", style=dashed];
    nexus -> node_c [label="strengthen", style=dashed];

```

A single binary is a complete execution node. The fleet model scales at two
levels:

- Instance level: each node is an independent process with its own memory
  space and thread pool. The multithreaded core already uses the cores of
  its machine; nothing is shared and nothing contends.
- Machine level: any number of nodes can run on one machine, each isolated
  from the others. There is no shared runtime, no shared interpreter state,
  and no scheduler to coordinate them; the operating system schedules
  independent processes, which it does well.

Deployment is orchestration-free. Copying the binary into a project root
makes it a node. There is no container image to build, no daemon to
install, no registry to join; the node exists because the file exists.

Coordination is by stigmergy through neXus. Nodes deposit facts and traces
in the shared coordinate space and read the deposits of others. A node in
project alpha records a finding; a node in project beta reads it and
adapts; a node in project gamma combines both and addresses a correction
to the common library. The fleet coordinates as peers, with no central
planner and no single point of failure.

## Linear Economics

```{python}
#| label: fig-telos-linear
#| fig-cap: "The unit economics of a fleet: per-node cost stays flat as nodes are added, and total cost grows as a straight line through the origin. Server and LLM spend scale with workload; the overhead terms stay constant."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams.update({"font.family": "sans-serif", "font.size": 9, "figure.dpi": 150})

fig, (ax_left, ax_right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.4))

fleet = np.arange(1, 21, dtype=float)

ax_left.plot(fleet, np.ones_like(fleet), color="#2c6f8f", linewidth=2)
ax_left.fill_between(fleet, 0.90, 1.10, color="#9ec9e8", alpha=0.35)
ax_left.set_xlabel("nodes in the fleet")
ax_left.set_ylabel("cost per node")
ax_left.set_title("per-node cost")
ax_left.set_xticks([1, 5, 10, 15, 20])
ax_left.set_ylim(0, 1.5)
ax_left.grid(alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.5)

ax_right.plot(fleet, fleet, color="#a06b8a", linewidth=2)
ax_right.fill_between(fleet, fleet * 0.90, fleet * 1.10, color="#d9b8c8", alpha=0.35)
ax_right.set_xlabel("nodes in the fleet")
ax_right.set_ylabel("total cost")
ax_right.set_title("total cost")
ax_right.set_xticks([1, 5, 10, 15, 20])
ax_right.set_ylim(0, 24)
ax_right.grid(alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.5)

fig.tight_layout()
```

The cost structure of a fleet is its defining property. Server spend and
LLM spend scale linearly with workload: doubling the fleet doubles the cost
and nothing else. The resources that grow are the ones the work consumes,
compute and tokens; the overhead terms stay constant. Each node's resource
use is bounded and predictable, so the unit economics hold from one node to
a thousand. Pricing can be set per call or per project without superlinear
cost growth.

## The tel Interface

`tel` is the command surface of the fleet. A command names a target: a
project root, a repository, a task. The nearest node picks up the command,
executes it, and streams the result back in real time. Command intake,
cancellation, and tool authorization arrive over the actus WebSocket
contract, so a run can be interrupted mid-execution and the node records
exactly where it stopped.

## Project-Root Deployment

Telos is designed to live in the project root, one binary per project.
There is no project file to open and no interface process to keep alive.
The presence of the binary in the root is the registration: the node is on
the network because it exists on disk.

Each node is bound to its tree by the operating system. A node in project
alpha cannot read the files of project beta, because there is no shared
process and no shared privilege. Nodes exchange only addressed facts and
traces through neXus, so the blast radius of a failure or a compromise
stays inside one project.

## Contract

Telos keeps a wire contract 1:1 with actus. Actus launches telos as its
agent binary; telos connects back over WebSocket, announces readiness, and
then serves commands and emits events. The contract is the only stable
boundary: eight event types flow from telos to actus, three command types
flow from actus to telos, and every consumer path in actus depends on their
semantics, including cumulative content overwrite, turn-end replay
filtering, and the one-terminal-event-per-request rule.

## Layers

| Layer | Project | Role |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Physical foundation | Chton (tagma) | coordinates over disk, RAM, and network bytes |
| Data hub | Nexus | logs, snapshots, and state over the coordinate space |
| Verification | EV and peers | mathematical verification of coordinate operations |
| Intelligence | Actus | planning with the LLM, domain knowledge |
| Execution | Telos | command intake, system call conversion, ACP/MCP execution |

## Status

Bootstrap. A self-contained agent core (`telos-core`) implements the
contract end to end: an LLM backend with a tool registry and a tool-call
loop. Without an API key the loop falls back to a canned backend, so the
actus chat flow works with this binary attached either way.

The headless binary runs the core directly (project, native agent, and
external websocket sync) with no interface stack, and ships with the
built-in model providers. The repository is private. Licensing is decided
only if and when distribution is planned.

## Direction

- The full tool surface: file, process, network, and MCP effects produced
  from resolved coordinates.
- Basic indexing integrated into tagma coordinates, so location resolution
  is arithmetic over coordinates rather than filesystem descent.
- Time teleport: neXus replay restores a previous execution state at fine
  granularity, coarser than a commit and cheaper than a checkout.
- Fleet operations: multi-node deployment, stigmergy coordination, and the
  `tel` command surface.
- The layer stays general: any LLM, any environment, any domain.
